transcript:
Meeting header: 2028-09-14 16:00 PDT | Duration: ~62m | Attendees: Maya (Redwood AE), Carlos (Redwood SE), Dana (Lucent Head of ML), Owen (SRE), Priya (Product), Greg (CTO)

Summary: Quick discovery + POC scoping focused on unit economics. Customer wants clarity on per-token math, batching/caching recommendations, and a benchmark window to validate latency and cost under realistic load.

00:00 Maya: Hey everyone, thanks for carving time. Quick intros? I'm Maya, AE at Redwood, and Carlos is our SE.
00:08 Dana: Hi, Dana here. I lead ML infra at Lucent.
00:11 Owen: Owen, SRE — network and security.
00:13 Priya: Priya, product — responsible for the user flows.
00:15 Greg: Greg, CTO — I'll be on the call for the economics and timeline bits.
00:19 Carlos: Great. Goal for today: align on success criteria, get the workload sizing, and agree a bench plan so we can model cost and propose a pilot.

02:05 Maya: Dana — can you paint high-level workload? QPS, average request length, and worst-case?
02:12 Dana: Sure, our primary use case is in-app summarization and a small gen assistant. Average prompt ~120 tokens in, we see about 0.6 requests per user per day currently. For pilot we'll simulate 10k DAUs, target concurrency around 80–120 active sessions, peak bursts maybe up to 300 concurrent. Latency target is 250–350ms p95 for short responses, tolerable up to 700ms for longer multi-turn.

04:01 Maya: Helpful. Do you have an expected output token size?
04:05 Dana: Baseline 80 tokens out, but some long docs can be 600 tokens; for the pilot we want to cap at 256.

05:18 Carlos: Okay, that tells us sequence length distribution. For the per-token econ we usually model three scenarios: baseline (no batching), optimized with batching and prefix/KV caching, and a heavy load with quantized model variant.
05:44 Owen: Quick security note — we need VPC mode or dedicated with customer-managed peering. SOC2 also required, plus key management; cannot send raw PII to hosted endpoints without encryption at rest and in transit.

06:12 Maya: We support Private/Dedicated with VPC peering and KMS integration. We'll send SOC2 docs after this call.

07:00 Priya: What's the expected $/token delta between hosted and dedicated? Rough number to justify budget.

07:20 Carlos: Roughly, hosted API list-pricing is typically higher per-token but includes multi-tenant amortization; Dedicated can drop unit cost by 35–65% depending on utilization and batching. Big drivers: sequence length, batch size, and cache hit rates. If you get a 40% prefix cache hit and steady batching at 16–32 tokens effective batch, you'll see major savings.

09:15 Greg: When you say cache hit — is that on the KV cache across sessions? Our prompts often start with a shared system prompt.
09:23 Carlos: Exactly, prefix caching/KV cache caches the transformer key/value pairs for repeated prepended system context, so if your first 50 tokens are identical across requests, that work is not recomputed. We sometimes call it K-V cash in quick notes, which is confusing in transcripts, ha.

11:48 Dana: Our flows have a stable system prompt and variable user prompt. We can easily get 45–55% prefix cache hit. What's the impact on p95?
11:58 Carlos: With cache hits, latency for cached prefixes drops dramatically — you only compute new tokens. We typically see p95 improve by 30–50% in those cases, and per-token compute cost is only for the suffix portion.

13:40 Owen: On capacity — do you provide autoscaling? For Dedicated we want predictable throughput but also burst buffer.
13:48 Maya: Yes, Dedicated has configurable autoscale + burst capacity. We can set guaranteed capacity for the pilot and a burst pool. Billing for burst is different but we model it in the cost spreadsheet.

15:30 Priya: For the bench, we want to validate: 1) p95 < 350ms for common flows, 2) cost per DAU under $0.06/mo in pilot assumptions, 3) no data egress violations. Are those reasonable success criteria?
15:45 Greg: Add quality checks — output similarity threshold vs our baseline — we don't want quantization degrading UX.

17:05 Carlos: Good call. We'll include rollout of model variants: fp16 and an int8 quantized variant. Benchmark will measure latency, token throughput, and quality via our similarity metric.

19:30 Dana: How do you set the per-token rate in the spreadsheet? I want to see both raw compute $/token and realized $/token after batching/cache/overhead.
19:42 Maya: Our spreadsheet shows raw compute (GPU hours -> token/sec -> $), then adds software/runtime overhead, networking, and support. Then we apply amortization for reserved capacity if you choose Dedicated. We'll produce three tables per scenario.

22:10 Owen: Concern — if our peak bursts are short, Dedicated amortization might be bad. How do you mitigate?
22:20 Carlos: We generally recommend a hybrid: Dedicated for baseline plus small hosted fallbacks for huge bursts. Smart routing can failover automatically to a compatible open model in hosted mode with throttling rules. That gets you predictable baseline cost with elastic headroom.

25:00 Priya: For the pilot timeline — how long to stand up a Dedicated pool and run bench?
25:10 Maya: Provisioning Dedicated with networking and KMS typically takes 2–3 weeks end-to-end if approvals are quick. Bench window is 1–2 days of active testing but we'll schedule a warm-up. For a fast pilot we can start with hosted in 48–72 hours to collect initial metrics, then migrate to Dedicated for the main bench.

28:40 Greg: What's your recommended batch size for our expected latency targets? We can't push batch size so high that p95 suffers.
28:50 Carlos: We'll target effective batching around 8–16 for p95 under 350ms for seq length ~256, with continuous batching on the runtime. If you can tolerate p95 up to 500ms, we can be more aggressive with batching (32+). We'll test multiple configs.

31:20 Dana: Any ops constraints we should know — memory, kv sizing, or eviction policies?
31:28 Carlos: You'll see KV cache per worker sized to typical prefix length; eviction is LRU per shard. We'll include recommended sizes in the bench plan. Also quantization reduces memory footprint but can increase CPU pre/post processing so we'll measure end-to-end.

34:55 Owen: Network — we require private peering with no public egress for pilot data. Can you support?
35:02 Maya: Yes, Private + VPC peering is supported. We'll add network steps in the runbook.

37:10 Priya: Okay, so immediate deliverables: cost model, bench plan, and a test corpus. Also, please include example alert thresholds and SLOs for operational monitoring.
37:25 Maya: Will do. Carlos will author the bench plan and include SLO templates.

40:40 Carlos: Bench plan outline I'll send: traffic profile generator, prompt distributions, warm-up, exact model variants (open-llama style / quantized), measurements (p50/p95/p99, tokens/sec, cost per 1k requests), and quality evaluation pipeline.

43:12 Greg: On quality evals — we'll provide a golden set and similarity thresholds. Can you run automatic drift checks?
43:20 Carlos: Yes, Redwood Optimize has eval hooks. For the pilot we'll run before/after comparisons and flag any regressions.

46:02 Dana: Pricing sensitivity — if quantized model gives small degradation, what are the savings? Ballpark percent?
46:10 Carlos: Int8 often saves 30–50% in compute cost vs fp16 with similar throughput; depends on kernel efficiency. We'll quantify for your exact model.

48:33 Priya: Anything else on legal or procurement? Owen mentioned SOC2; also need DPA language and data retention policies.
48:44 Maya: We'll share DPA and retention options. For Private deployments we can do customer-managed logging and retention windows.

52:05 Greg: I want to align on success criteria in writing after this call so our finance team can sign off. Can you produce a one-pager that maps metrics to go/no-go?
52:15 Maya: Yes — a Go/No-Go checklist with thresholds and estimated monthly $ impact. We'll send with the cost workbook.

57:30 Dana: Quick question — are model updates during pilot included? If we need a patch or different model, how disruptive is that?
57:42 Carlos: We support canary rollouts and A/B. Model swaps are managed by the control plane; we can route a percentage of traffic to new variant for short windows. Should be non-disruptive if planned.

60:20 Maya: Ok, let's recap next steps: Maya sends cost workbook + SOC2 links; Carlos sends bench plan and scripts; Priya shares prompt set and sample queries; Owen sends VPC details; Greg to confirm success criteria. We'll target the bench week starting 2028-09-21.

61:10 Greg: Sounds good. Thanks everyone.
61:15 Maya: Thanks — we'll follow up in email with links and ask for any additional constraints.
61:22 End of recording.
